issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access' conflicts with the other memory items. Being able to talk about the rape very easily is hard to reconcile with a profile centered on fragmented, unreal, image-based trauma memory and severe PTSD symptoms.

issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Story Feels Unreal' and 'Snapshot Memory' suggest poorly elaborated, emotionally overwhelming trauma memory, which clashes with 'Verbal Access'. This makes the Memory node internally inconsistent.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability' is less coherent with the rest of the profile because the dominant appraisals are global loss and mistrust, while the reported threat pattern is generalized anticipatory danger rather than fear specifically tied to bodily injury. For rape it is possible, but here it is the least well integrated appraisal relative to the other selected items.

vignette: María is a forty-seven-year-old married woman who works as a social ministry coordinator at a Catholic parish in a mid-sized city. She came to therapy at the urging of her husband, who had grown increasingly worried about the changes he had seen in her over the past eighteen months. The change began on a Tuesday evening in late spring, when she stayed late at the church rectory to prepare food baskets for a community outreach program. A man she recognized from the neighborhood—someone who had occasionally come to the parish seeking assistance—found her alone in the kitchen. What María remembers of the assault is not a continuous story but a series of frozen moments: the pressure of his hand over her mouth, the linoleum tile pattern against her cheek, the sound of a metal chair scraping across the floor. She cannot find the words to describe what happened between those images, and when she tries, her throat closes and she goes silent. What she does feel, every time the memory surfaces, is a crushing guilt—a certainty that she should have known better, should have locked the door, should have screamed louder. She has come to believe that she is no longer the person she used to be. She used to be joyful, quick to laugh, the kind of woman who organized parish picnics and visited the homebound with a thermos of soup. Now she feels hollowed out, and she has lost her faith in people, in the goodness she once took for granted. She is deeply ashamed of what happened to her body, as though her skin itself has been marked. That shame has reshaped her daily life. When she cannot find words to describe the event, the guilt deepens, and she tells herself she deserves to suffer, so she has stopped allowing herself small pleasures—she restricts her eating with rigid control, skipping meals as a kind of penance. She has also stopped relaxing, because letting her guard down feels like an invitation for something terrible to happen again. The parish priest has accommodated her request to work only during daylight hours and to never be alone in the building, but even in her own home, with her husband beside her on the couch, she cannot relax. She finds herself hyperalert to unusual silence—when the television goes quiet between programs, or when the house settles at night, her heart pounds and she is certain that something dangerous is about to emerge from the stillness. When her husband is late coming home from work, even by ten minutes, her mind races with catastrophic scenarios. The more she monitors the world for threat, the more convinced she becomes that she is fundamentally unsafe, and that her body is ruined and shameful. The avoidance itself feeds back into the memory: every time she restricts a meal or refuses to sit still, she is reminded of why she must do these things, and the snapshots of that night flash more vividly. The cycle has tightened over many months. She has stopped attending the larger parish events she once loved, telling herself she is too tired, though what she really fears is the press of a crowd or the sudden silence of a hallway. Her husband has noticed that she no longer touches him the way she used to, and she has not been able to explain why. She finally agreed to come to therapy because last week, during a routine meeting with a parishioner, the man cleared his throat and the sound—a dry, scraping noise—sent her back to that linoleum floor, and she excused herself and vomited in the bathroom. She is afraid that she is losing herself completely, but what frightens her most is the possibility that she might never feel safe again, and that she might be right to believe she does not deserve to.
